intro.title: Help
intro.description: Quick guide to every menu in the application, plus the list of system dependencies required for the tool to work correctly on the server (Raspberry Pi or Ubuntu/Debian).

dashboard.summary: Home screen: server health at a glance.
details: CPU, RAM, disk, and temperature gauges update in real time over WebSocket.
An alert banner appears automatically when a critical threshold is crossed (temperature, disk full, etc.).
Click an alert to see its detail in the System screen.

docker.summary: Full management of containers, images, volumes, and networks.
details: Containers tab: start/stop/restart/remove, view live logs and CPU/RAM stats, a "Backup" button that opens Applications pre-filled.
Images tab: export an image to .tar (downloadable), import a .tar, delete.
Volumes tab: back up in one click, restore the latest backup, delete.
Networks tab: list of configured Docker networks.

nginx.summary: Web server administration: sites, configuration, certificates.
details: List of vhosts with enabled/disabled status, ports, proxy target, and site folder location.
Each site has a clickable link that opens it in a new tab, a real HTTP accessibility test, traffic for the last 7 days, and recent errors.
Configuration editing with automatic validation (nginx -t) before applying — a version history lets you roll back.
SSL certificate status (Let's Encrypt or manual certificate) with expiration date.
Full backup of the Nginx configuration (local and/or Google Drive).

sites.summary: Combined view of a site: its Nginx config, its associated Docker container, and duplication for failover.
details: Useful to quickly find everything about a site without navigating between two screens.

"Clone" button: creates a full duplicate of the site (content folder, database if selected, and a second container on a different port if the site uses a Docker container) — a standby copy ready to take over.

"Switch to duplicate" button: redirects all site traffic to this copy in one click, useful in case of an outage or system error on the primary site. The action is reversible via "Switch back to primary".
The duplicate is a frozen snapshot at the time it was created — later changes to the original are not automatically reflected in it. Use "Update from original" to resync it.
You cannot fail over a site currently in maintenance mode (exit maintenance first) — the two states cannot be active at the same time.

os.summary: Updates and packages for the Debian system.
details: List of installed packages and those with an available update.
Check for updates and apply them (upgrade/full-upgrade) with live progress tracking.
Management of "held" packages (pinned, excluded from updates).

pm2.summary: Node.js applications running directly on the server (outside Docker), managed by PM2.
details: List of processes with status, CPU, RAM, uptime, and restart count.
Start/stop/restart/reload actions and live log viewing.
Node.js apps running inside a Docker container remain managed from the Docker screen.

network.summary: Network exposure, IP blocking, and hardware information about the server.
details: Open ports on the machine, with the owning process or container.
Blocking/unblocking IP addresses via fail2ban.
System tab: hardware model (on Raspberry Pi: supply voltage and throttling), date/time and timezone, network interfaces and IPs, Wi-Fi (scan and connect), SSH status, active and failed services.

applications.summary: The most complete backup system: container + folders + volumes + database bundled together.
details: An "Application" links one or more containers, their disk-mounted folders (bind mounts), their named Docker volumes, and an optional database.

Full backup: a complete snapshot, including an image export of each container (so everything can be recreated even if the original image is lost). Partial backup: only copies files that are new/changed since the last snapshot (saves disk space, no image export).
Can be scheduled automatically (e.g. daily partial, weekly full) via simple presets.
An application can also have only a database, with no folder or volume, if the container is stateless (e.g. a plain reverse proxy).
This screen is only for creating/managing backups — to restore, go to the Restore screen.

backups.summary: Creation and deletion of one-off or scheduled backups of volumes, folders, and databases.
details: Two steps: choose the type (Full, or Partial for a database dump), then the destination (local, USB if a drive is plugged in, Google Drive if connected, and/or direct download to your device).
A plugged-in USB/SSD drive is detected and mounted automatically — backups are stored in a folder dedicated to this server.
History of every backup with deletion available (the local file is deleted; existing USB/Drive copies are untouched).
This screen no longer offers any restore action — that's deliberate, to avoid an accidental click that would overwrite data. Restoring is done exclusively from the Restore screen.
Copy encryption, the encrypted (LUKS) USB drive, reading it on another computer and troubleshooting: see the "Backups, encryption and the USB drive" guide further down this page.

restore.summary: Guided 3-step restore, the only place in the application where data can be overwritten.
details: Step 1: choose the source — Local (backups already on this server), USB (a plugged-in drive containing archives), Google Drive, or upload a backup file from your PC/phone.
Step 2: choose the exact item to restore, grouped by category (databases, volumes, folders, container images, full/partial applications) to stay readable even with many archives.
Step 3: explicit confirmation (type "RESTORE") before any irreversible action.

Restoring a container image causes no service interruption on failure: the new container is created and verified before the old one is stopped — if recreation fails, the running application stays intact.
An archive found on a USB drive with no known history (e.g. after a full reinstall) can be imported directly from this screen to become restorable.

system.summary: Detailed monitoring beyond the Dashboard gauges.
details: Per-disk and per-network-interface detail, throttling/under-voltage status, operating system information.

cleanup.summary: Disk scan and cleanup of temporary files, caches, old logs and old local backups.
details: "Scan the server" measures what can be freed without deleting anything: the application's working files, the service account's temporary files, the npm cache, unused Docker images and build cache, downloaded apt packages, old system logs and old local backups.
Each category is marked "Safe" (rebuilds itself) or "Review" (old backups, logs); only the safe ones are ticked by default. The biggest items can be inspected before cleaning.
Old backups: choose the age (30 days by default). The newest backups of each source are always kept, and copies on USB and Google Drive are never touched.
Never touched: installed packages, kernels, Docker volumes, stopped containers, databases. Cleaning apt packages and logs needs the sudo rules installed by deploy/install.sh.
The "Where local backup space goes" block shows the size of each data/backups folder.

services.summary: Status and update actions for services installed on the server (Tailscale, Docker, PM2).
details: Each service shows whether it's installed, running, its version, and a few extra details (container count, process count, etc.).
Available actions: update Tailscale, update or restart Docker (restart = brief interruption of all containers), reload the PM2 daemon.
The result of each action (output of the executed command) stays viewable to diagnose a possible failure.
Enable 2FA (recommended) via a QR code to scan with an authenticator app.
Audit log listing every sensitive action performed (who, what, when, result).
Backup copy encryption: choose whether new USB and Google Drive copies are encrypted with the application's key.

backupGuide.heading: Backups, encryption and the USB drive: complete guide
backupGuide.intro: Everything you need to back up, protect and recover your data, including without the application.

cards.title: Overview: where are my backups and how are they protected?
cards.summary: Three independent layers of protection, to combine as you need.

blocks.text: A backup can exist in three places, each with its own protection:

items: Local copy (the server's data/backups folder): never encrypted. It serves quick restores and protects against handling mistakes, not against theft or loss of the server.
Copy on a USB/SSD drive: can be protected in two ways that stack — each archive encrypted with the application's key (Settings option), and the whole drive encrypted with LUKS.
Copy on Google Drive: encrypted with the application's key (Settings option). While the option is on, Google cannot read it.

blocks.text: Recommended combinations:

items: Encrypted (LUKS) USB drive and USB archive encryption off: simple, and the drive is unreadable if lost or stolen (locked or unplugged).
Unencrypted USB drive: keep archive encryption on.
Google Drive: always keep archive encryption on.

blocks.text: While a LUKS drive is unlocked and mounted (the normal state for scheduled backups), anyone with access to the server can read its files. Archive encryption protects in that case too.
The migration bundle (Backups → "Server migration") is not encrypted archive by archive on the USB drive: put it on a LUKS drive, or delete it after use.
Backups are stored on the USB drive in BACKUP/<server-name>/ with the folders volumes, paths (folders and container images), db (databases), apps (applications) and migration.

cards.title: Archive encryption (the application's key)
cards.summary: How USB and Drive copies are encrypted, the private key, and how to restore.

blocks.text: On first start the application creates a key pair. The public key encrypts each archive copied to USB or uploaded to Google Drive; every file gets its own random secret (X25519 + AES-256-GCM, Node.js's built-in crypto). The result is a .tar.gz.enc file, unreadable without the private key, and any tampering is detected.
The private key is kept on the server (secrets/backup-encryption.private, mode 0600) so restores from the application work without asking. It is never written to the USB drive or to Drive.

blocks.title: Make your own copy of the key (essential):
items: Backups, card "Keep a copy of your private encryption key": click "Show private key".
Copy or download it and store it away from the server (password manager, printout).
Tick "I have saved this key somewhere safe" then "Confirm".

blocks.text: If the server is destroyed and you have no copy of the key, the encrypted archives on USB and Drive are permanently unreadable.

items: Options: Settings → "Backup copy encryption" lets you encrypt or not the new USB and/or Drive copies. It only affects new copies; older ones stay readable with the key.

Restoring: Restore → USB or Google Drive. With the key on the server everything is automatic. If the key is no longer on this server or doesn't match the archive (it came from another server), the application asks you to paste the private key (format pwa-admin-key-v1:…). It is sent once and not stored.
"Remove the key from this server" button (available once your copy is confirmed): optional hardening — restores will then always ask for the key.
Limit: a file larger than 60 GB cannot be encrypted. Local copies are never encrypted.

cards.title: Encrypted USB drive (LUKS)
cards.summary: Encrypt the whole drive, unlock it, eject it and reconnect it.

blocks.text: LUKS is Linux's standard disk encryption: without the passphrase (or the keyfile), a drive plugged into another computer is just unreadable data.

blocks.title: Encrypt a drive (Backups → "USB / SSD drive" card):
items: Click "Encrypt this drive (LUKS)". WARNING: this erases everything on the drive.
Enter a passphrase twice (at least 8 characters) and write it down away from the server.
Choose automatic unlock (keyfile stored on the server) or not.
Type the partition name (for example sda1) to confirm, then "Erase and encrypt". Allow several minutes and keep the page open.
Once the drive is mounted, click "Activate" to make it the backup drive.

blocks.text: The drive is formatted as LUKS2 with an ext4 filesystem (name BACKUP) mounted on /media/backup-usb. Badges show its state: "Not encrypted" (grey), "Encrypted · unlocked" (green, usable), "Encrypted · locked" (orange, passphrase needed).

items: Automatic unlock: a keyfile (/etc/pwa-admin/usb-luks.key, readable by root only) opens the drive when plugged in. Handy for scheduled backups, but the key is on the server: it protects against losing the drive alone, not against the server being stolen along with it. Can be turned on or off later with the passphrase.
Without automatic unlock: enter the passphrase each time you plug the drive in ("Encrypted USB drive is locked" card). While it is locked, scheduled USB copies are skipped.
Eject: unmounts the drive and closes the encrypted volume; you can then unplug it safely.
Reconnect: mounts a still-plugged-in drive again after an eject, without unplugging it (encrypted drive with automatic unlock, or unencrypted drive). Otherwise use "Unlock" with the passphrase.
Reformat: on a locked encrypted drive (lost passphrase, interrupted format), erases everything and starts over.

blocks.text: Lost passphrase = drive permanently unreadable, with no recourse. Never unplug the drive during a backup, a format or an automatic-unlock change: always use "Eject".

System protection: a server that boots from a USB SSD (for example a Raspberry Pi) never offers its own disk. Any partition of a disk that hosts the system is excluded from activation, encryption, formatting and reconnect.

cards.title: Reading a LUKS drive on another computer

blocks.text: The drive holds a LUKS partition with an ext4 filesystem inside. You need the passphrase.
Linux (easiest): the file manager (Nautilus, Dolphin…) detects the drive, asks for the passphrase and mounts it. On the command line (replace sdX1 with the drive's partition, found with lsblk):

lines: sudo umount /mnt/backup && sudo cryptsetup close backup

blocks.text: Windows cannot read LUKS and will offer to format the drive: always answer "Cancel". Two options: boot the PC from a Linux USB stick (Ubuntu, "Try without installing") and follow the Linux method; or use WSL2 (Windows 10 21H2 or later, Windows 11) in a PowerShell run as administrator:

lines: Get-CimInstance Win32_DiskDrive | Select-Object DeviceID, Model, Size

blocks.text: Replace 2 with the drive's number (about the size of the T7). Then, inside WSL (Ubuntu), use the Linux commands above: your files appear in Explorer under \\wsl$\Ubuntu\mnt\backup. To detach the drive afterwards:
If cryptsetup fails under WSL (dm-crypt module missing), update WSL with "wsl --update".
macOS: no native support. Use a Linux virtual machine with access to the USB device, or boot a PC from a Linux stick.
VeraCrypt, BitLocker and "ext4 for Windows" drivers cannot read LUKS.

cards.title: Opening a .tar.gz.enc archive outside the application
cards.summary: Decrypt by hand with the standalone tool and the private key.

blocks.text: If the application is no longer available (destroyed server, fresh install…), you can decrypt an archive with the standalone decrypt-backup.mjs tool: it needs Node.js 16 or newer and nothing else. Download it with the button below (or from the repository, folder apps/web/public/tools).

blocks.title: Decrypt an archive:
items: Save your private key in a text file, for example key.txt (a single line: pwa-admin-key-v1:…).
Run the decryption, then extract the resulting archive:

lines: mkdir restored && tar xzf archive.tar.gz -C restored

blocks.text: Decryption checks integrity: if the key is wrong, or the file is modified or truncated, the tool refuses and leaves no output file. The key can also come from the PWA_BACKUP_KEY environment variable (avoid the --key option, which stays in your shell history).
An archive without .enc unpacks directly with tar. Exception: database backups (names ending in .dump.gz.tar.gz) are a plain gzip stream holding the dump, despite the extension:
For a LUKS drive, unlock the drive first (previous section), then decrypt the .enc archives it contains if archive encryption was on.

cards.title: Troubleshooting
cards.summary: Common problems with the USB drive and encryption.

items: "No USB drive detected": drive unplugged, or a system disk (never offered). Plug it in; if it is encrypted and locked, the "Encrypted USB drive is locked" card appears.
"Wrong passphrase": check what you typed (capitals, keyboard layout). Without the right passphrase there is no way to read the drive.

The drive disconnects during a large write: a USB 3 link problem. Try another cable or port, and disable UAS mode for this drive; on very recent hardware, use a recent Linux kernel. The kernel log (journalctl -k) shows xhci/usb errors.

Ghost volume after an abrupt unplug: the application normally cleans these up when the drive is plugged back in. By hand: sudo umount -l /media/backup-usb then sudo cryptsetup close backup-usb-crypt (or sudo dmsetup remove --force backup-usb-crypt).
Restore asks for the private key: the key is no longer on this server, or the archive comes from another server. Paste the original server's key.
"The drive is encrypted but has no readable filesystem": interrupted format. Use "Reformat".
After an application update: re-run deploy/install.sh on the server to update the USB drive scripts (mounting, LUKS tool, sudo rules). A plain git pull is not enough.

tips: The server icon in the top right lets you save multiple deployments (e.g. a Raspberry Pi and an Ubuntu server) and quickly switch between them — each remains an independent installation with its own connection.
Pull the screen down from the top of a page and hold for a few seconds to force a full reload of the application — useful to get the latest version after an update.
dependenciesIntro: These programs must be present on the server for the corresponding modules to work. Most are already standard on Raspberry Pi OS / Debian / Ubuntu.

docker.name: Docker
docker.purpose: Required for the Docker module and volume/container backups.

nginx.name: Nginx
nginx.purpose: Required for the Nginx module and site monitoring.

systemd.name: systemd
systemd.purpose: Manages the application service and the services listed in Network & Security.

sudo.name: sudo + scoped rules
sudo.purpose: Allows privileged actions (reload nginx, apt, etc.) without running the service as root.

vcgencmd.name: vcgencmd (Raspberry Pi OS/firmware)
vcgencmd.purpose: Temperature, voltage, and throttling — specific to Raspberry Pi hardware.

networkmanager.name: NetworkManager (nmcli)
networkmanager.purpose: Wi-Fi management (scan, connect) in Network & Security.

openssh.name: openssh-server
openssh.purpose: SSH access and status shown in Network & Security.

pm2.name: PM2
pm2.purpose: Required for the Node.js (PM2) module if Node apps run outside Docker.

database.name: MariaDB / MySQL / PostgreSQL / Redis (optional)
database.purpose: Auto-detected if installed natively, for database backups.

rsync.name: rsync
rsync.purpose: Used by the Applications module for full/partial snapshots.

tailscale.name: Tailscale
tailscale.purpose: Secure network access — the app must never be exposed publicly.
